title: Commissioners’ votes on matters with a connected party
question: When a party before the Planning Commission, the Historic Preservation Commission or the Board of Appeals had given to the mayor who appointed a member, or paid that member, how did the member vote?
finding: 170 decisions at the three bodies have a party whose wanted outcome is on record (a lobbyist’s client citing the case number, or an organization named as appellant or permit holder), giving 1,131 member votes. Comparing like with like, for members whose appointing Mayor or President of the Board can be named: at the Planning Commission members voted the party’s way in 78 of 78 votes where the party was in the appointing official’s donor circle (100.0%) and in 98.0% of the other 500 (within what chance would produce); at the Historic Preservation Commission members voted the party’s way in 4 of 4 votes where the party was in the appointing official’s donor circle (100.0%) and in 100.0% of the other 26 (too few cases to test); at the Board of Appeals members voted the party’s way in 0 of 2 votes where the party was in the appointing official’s donor circle (0.0%) and in 55.6% of the other 234 (too few cases to test). In 0 votes the party was an income source the member had declared; 85 recusals are printed in the same minutes.
how: Planning and Historic Preservation Commission votes are the ayes and noes printed in the minutes of January 2019 to August 2022 on actions that approve or disapprove; a party is the client of a lobbyist whose reported contact cites the same planning case number and asks for approval or opposition in the three years before the hearing. Board of Appeals votes are those in the minutes of September 2022 to November 2026 on motions to grant or deny an appeal; parties are organizations printed as appellant (wanting it granted) or as permit holder (wanting it denied); individuals are left out. Each member is tied by surname to the Board file recording the appointment, which names the nominating official: a Mayor (the Mayor on the day the file was introduced) or the President of the Board (the name on the Board’s agendas around that date). “Donor circle” means the party, or donors naming it as employer, gave to that official’s committees before the hearing. “Declared income” is the member’s own Form 700 Schedule C.
limits: Being connected is not being corrupt. Nearly every commission vote is to approve, and lobbyists’ clients are mostly applicants asking for approval, so voting a party’s way is the normal outcome whether or not the party ever gave to anyone. Commissioners are matched by surname as the minutes print it, to the appointment file nearest before the vote or the earliest on disk; members appointed before 2015, by the Board as a whole, or by a President who cannot be named from the agendas, have no appointing official here. The minutes on disk cover 2019 to 2022 for the commissions and 2022 to 2026 for the Board of Appeals only. Parties are matched by exact name. Amounts, parties and dates taken from Board file titles are read by machine: in a hand check of 50 titles, 11 had at least one field read wrongly (4 after later fixes).
